stops.name: Oslo, the school of movement, the therapy of the dance
stops.campa: She begins again, teaching. For years after the war Elsa teaches a form of dance therapy shaped by Reich's psychiatric concepts, the work she made beside him in the golden years, now hers alone: tension and release, breath and expression, the armor read in the moving body. In Norway the lineage she planted flows into the country's own school of the body: Bülow-Hansen, Braatøy, the psychomotor tradition. A form of her dance-movement work is practiced there still. The canon calls her a founding mother of the discipline.

stops.name: Oslo, rehabilitated, the state's pension
stops.campa: The state makes its amends: Elsa Lindenberg is rehabilitated by the Norwegian government and awarded a state pension. The file that began with a Berlin warrant in 1933, enemy of the German state, then enemy German, closes at last with a Norwegian apology and a monthly sum. She accepts it as she accepted the scholarship at thirteen: as owed to the body that earned it. Oslo is now, finally and officially, her city, and will be to the end.

stops.name: Berlin, Gindler again
stops.campa: She returns to Berlin, the wound inspected once more, to study again with Elsa Gindler, her teacher before the war and after it, who has survived the destruction of her studio and teaches on amid the rubble-city. The quiet work resumes as if twenty years of catastrophe were an interruption between two breaths. Lindenberg carries the Gindler method back north and becomes, in Oslo, its much-respected teacher: guardian of a doctrine that was never written down.

stops.name: Oslo, the chair and the swan
stops.campa: A car accident has broken her hip and ended her dancing; Elsa leads her Oslo classes from a chair, grey-haired and heavy now, scolding her students, physiotherapists who come to her secretly, against their teacher's moral disapproval of the unwed wife, for moving without feeling. One day, failing to explain in words, she rises from the chair and dances. The grey duckling, Berit Bunkan will remember, became a beautiful swan, soft, fantastic and elegant, and the students wept. Then she sits back down. The lesson is complete.

stops.name: Oslo, the small flat, Willy's picture
stops.campa: In a small Oslo flat, a picture of Wilhelm Reich on the wall beside her chair, Elsa receives visitors as Willy's second wife and rules the Scandinavian body-work as its dowager. When Miriam Goldberg comes from Israel to teach, Elsa summons her and asks, terribly, how she dares bring Charlotte Selver's method into her domain in short courses that can do damage. The room is electric; the visitors stand. The guardianship is absolute: what Gindler never wrote down, Lindenberg will not see cheapened.

stops.name: Oslo, Sharaf's visit
stops.campa: Myron Sharaf, writing the great biography of Reich, comes to Oslo and finds her at seventy strikingly attractive and vivacious. She speaks of Willy with tenderness, passion, humor and criticism at once: the jealous rages, the affairs, the abrupt ending after the passionate letters of 1939, all folded into a deep, genuine and unsentimental love. After Reich, she tells him, there was never another serious man; she was in her early thirties when they parted. Her testimony becomes a wellspring of the canon itself: Fury on Earth speaks with her voice.

stops.name: Lovisenberg Hospital, the last interview
stops.campa: In the early summer of 1990, old and ill in Lovisenberg Hospital, Elsa gives her last interview, to the Swedish journalist Anna Britta Staal with Berit Bunkan at the bedside. Pale in the bed, she begins to speak of Willy and her eyes sparkle, her face turns lively and rosy; she remembers the free sexuality of the golden household, where everything was natural. And she leaves the record one final correction: her last word on the hardest no ever said.
stops.quote: People think it was because of disagreement about the therapy that I did not go with Willy to USA, but that was not the reason.
stops.quote_source: Last interview, Lovisenberg Hospital, Oslo, summer 1990; recorded by Berit Heir Bunkan

stops.name: Oslo, the death of the dancer
stops.campa: On the sixth of November 1990 Elsa Lindenberg dies in Oslo, eighty-four years old, fifty-one years after the quay. Her papers pass to her friend Ida Korsvold, who lets no one see them: the archive keeps its silence like Gindler's unwritten method, and the biographers must make do with everyone else's letters. What cannot be sealed is the inheritance: body psychotherapy and dance-movement therapy, the two children of the union of the doctor and the dancer, both alive, both still moving.
